title: Classical guitar
summary: One string sounds at a time, and there is no A or D string. The body follows the plan of a 1964 Madrid guitar, not the recordings' Raimundo 118. The attack is too weak in the top octaves, E2 rings too long, and the body's low air tone dies away too slowly, and we can't yet say why. The nylon trebles and the wound E2 pluck a braced spruce top, rosewood back and ribs, a rosewood bridge and the air inside, with a computed air load acting on the shell and sound hole. G3, B3, E4 and Gb4 also carry viscoelastic bending loss, air loading on the string and longitudinal string modes; E2 and F5 don't have the last two. Ours is tuned to equal temperament and the recordings sit flat of it, so most of each pitch gap is theirs. The arpeggio and chord add separate renders, which don't exchange energy.
physics_present: The strings: nylon G3, B3 and E4 open, Gb4 and F5 stopped on the B string, and a wound E2 that takes its tension, line mass and bending stiffness whole from Woodhouse's 2004 measurement of one D'Addario set
Two polarizations on every string, with 24 bending modes per polarization on the nylon strings and 96 on E2
Tension on the open trebles comes from tuning the model to equal temperament on an earlier card, so no recording sets a value. They sit within a few cents of it on these cards
The string modes above the kept set carry their exact static compliance into the bridge (residual flexibility)
On G3, B3, E4 and Gb4: viscoelastic bending loss from the pack's cited Kelvin-Voigt row, air loading on the string (cylinder-gas-loading 0.3 30 4) and longitudinal string modes
On E2: the friction and bending loss factors Woodhouse fitted to that string
The body of the 1964 Madrid guitar in Zimmer and Mores' 2024 plan: a braced Sitka spruce top with its sound hole, a barred rosewood back, rosewood ribs and a rosewood bridge, with 128 body modes
Wood constants from the Wood Handbook (FPL-GTR-282), with wood loss measured on other samples
A boundary-element air load on the shell and sound-hole port (body-radiation skin, 20-1100 Hz). It changes how the body moves, not how the note is picked up
The enclosed air with a radiating sound-hole neck, whose outer end takes its mass and radiation from that air load
A compact receiver at 1 m at every frequency, on a 96 kHz clock
physics_missing: The other strings: one sounds at a time, so nothing rings in sympathy, and A2 and D3 aren't rendered. The arpeggio and chord add posted clips, with no coupling through the bridge or body and a balance taken from each page's recording

The string modes above the kept set: partials stop at the 24th on the nylon strings and at the 96th on E2, which takes the top of the attack with them. On G3, B3 and E4 a faint line above the last partial isn't a partial: the kept modes move together on the bridge's flexibility, an artefact of the cut

Body modes above the 128 kept, and a converged body mesh. The body's resonances stop near 1770 Hz, and 2 kHz is the most the wood packs allow: their moduli come from the Wood Handbook's static values. A no-skin test with 148 modes moved the partials near the cut in both directions, and on Gb4 brought the octave closer through a partial the recording barely has, so more modes alone isn't a fix

The air tone's loss: the body's low air resonance dies away more slowly than the recording's on G3, B3, E4, Gb4 and F5. The hole's edge loss isn't on these cards, and it wouldn't close the gap by itself. The rest is unexplained
G3's string: the recording's string is far less stiff than the printed nylon of this gauge, which suggests a different string; we have no print for it

E2 is one measured set's whole-string coefficients, not its construction: the core and winding are unknown, and its diameter, which sets only its air drag, is a stand-in from another gauge. Its level falls far more slowly than the Iowa E2's on the posted clips
The nylon's tension loss enters as zero, because the evidence table has no nylon row
The pluck: one point at one station, released from a static force, not measured on the recordings' player. No print gives the place on a stopped note. A finger or nail's width isn't modelled
Finger and fret contact on stopped notes (the fret is a rigid pinned end), and the player holding the guitar: ours hangs free
The string meets the body through an authored penalty spring (100000 N/m), not the saddle's contact mechanics

The body is one 1964 Madrid guitar's plan, not the Raimundo 118. Each part has one thickness. The neck and heel, blocks, linings, rosette, fingerboard, bridge patch, string holes, back strip and patches, glue and finish are left out
The plan names no bridge wood and prints no bridge position: rosewood is assumed and the station inferred
The air load stops at 1100 Hz, and the receiver is compact at every frequency, not a boundary-element microphone
Geometric stretching of the string isn't enabled: it's an alternative to the longitudinal waves, with no published coefficient
The output is 16-bit at a full scale of 1 Pa, so the quietest top-band content sits at the quantisation floor
